subject: Physics
title: Light - Reflection and Refraction - Complete Learning Module
outcomes: State and apply the laws of reflection
Describe the terms and image formation of concave and convex spherical mirrors
Apply the mirror formula and magnification with the Cartesian sign convention
Explain refraction and use the refractive index to relate speed and bending
Apply the lens formula and magnification for convex and concave lenses
Calculate the power of a lens and the power of lenses in contact
Solve board-style numericals on mirrors, lenses, and refraction

concepts.title: Reflection of Light and the Laws of Reflection
concepts.explanation: Light is a form of energy that travels in straight lines in a homogeneous medium. When it strikes a polished surface, it bounces back; this is reflection. The incident ray, the reflected ray, and the normal at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane. The angle of incidence is always equal to the angle of reflection. Regular reflection from a smooth surface gives a clear image, while diffused reflection from a rough surface scatters light in many directions.
key_points: Angle of incidence equals angle of reflection.
Incident ray, reflected ray, and normal lie in the same plane.
Regular reflection forms images; diffused reflection makes objects visible from all directions.
A plane mirror forms a virtual, erect image of the same size, with lateral inversion.
concepts.real_life_example: A bathroom mirror reflects light regularly and gives a clear image, while a rough wall reflects light diffusely and does not form an image.

concepts.title: Spherical Mirrors and Image Formation
concepts.explanation: A spherical mirror is a part of a hollow sphere whose one surface is silvered. A concave mirror has its reflecting surface curved inward, while a convex mirror has it curved outward. The pole is the centre of the mirror, the centre of curvature is the centre of the sphere, and the principal focus is the point where rays parallel to the principal axis meet or appear to meet after reflection. The focal length is half the radius of curvature, f = R/2 for a mirror of small aperture. Concave mirrors can form real or virtual images, but a convex mirror always forms a virtual, erect, and diminished image.
key_points: A concave mirror converges parallel rays; a convex mirror diverges them.
For a spherical mirror of small aperture, f = R/2.
A concave mirror forms real or virtual images depending on the object distance.
Concave mirrors are used in torches and shaving mirrors; convex mirrors in rear-view and security mirrors.
concepts.real_life_example: A convex rear-view mirror in a car always gives an erect, diminished image and a wide field of view behind the vehicle.

concepts.title: Mirror Formula and Magnification
concepts.explanation: The mirror formula relates object distance u, image distance v, and focal length f as 1/v + 1/u = 1/f. Distances are measured from the pole using the Cartesian sign convention: distances measured along the incident light are negative, and those measured opposite to it are positive. Magnification is m = -v/u = height of image / height of object. A negative magnification means a real, inverted image, while a positive magnification means a virtual, erect image.
key_points: Mirror formula: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f.
Object distance u is negative for a real object in front of the mirror.
Magnification: m = -v/u = h'/h.
Negative m means real and inverted; positive m means virtual and erect.
concepts.real_life_example: A concave shaving mirror held close to the face gives an erect, magnified virtual image because the face lies within the focal length.

concepts.title: Refraction and Refractive Index
concepts.explanation: Refraction is the bending of light as it passes from one transparent medium to another because its speed changes. When light enters an optically denser medium, it slows down and bends towards the normal; when it enters a rarer medium, it speeds up and bends away from the normal. Snell's law states that sin i / sin r is constant for a given pair of media. The absolute refractive index is n = c/v, where c is the speed of light in vacuum and v is the speed in the medium.
key_points: Refraction occurs because the speed of light changes between media.
Snell's law: n1 sin i = n2 sin r, or sin i / sin r = n21.
Absolute refractive index n = c/v; it is greater than 1 for any material medium.
Light bends towards the normal when entering a denser medium and away from it when entering a rarer medium.
concepts.real_life_example: A straw in a glass of water appears bent at the water surface because light from the submerged part refracts as it leaves water and enters air.

concepts.title: Spherical Lenses and the Lens Formula
concepts.explanation: A lens is a transparent refracting medium bounded by two spherical surfaces. A convex lens is thicker in the middle and converges parallel rays, while a concave lens is thinner in the middle and diverges them. The lens formula is 1/v - 1/u = 1/f, using the same Cartesian sign convention as mirrors. Magnification is m = v/u; a negative m gives a real inverted image and a positive m gives a virtual erect image.
key_points: A convex lens is converging and a concave lens is diverging.
Lens formula: 1/v - 1/u = 1/f.
Magnification: m = v/u = h'/h.
A convex lens forms real images for objects beyond f and virtual images for objects within f; a concave lens always forms virtual, erect, diminished images.
concepts.real_life_example: A magnifying glass is a convex lens; when the object is inside its focal length it gives an erect, enlarged virtual image.

concepts.title: Power of a Lens and Its Applications
concepts.explanation: The power of a lens measures its ability to converge or diverge light and is defined as P = 1/f, where f is the focal length in metres. Its SI unit is the dioptre (D), and 1 D = 1 m^-1. A convex lens has positive power and a concave lens has negative power. When thin lenses are placed in contact, their powers add: P = P1 + P2 + ..., which is used in spectacles and camera lenses.
key_points: Power P = 1/f, with f in metres.
SI unit of power is the dioptre, D.
Convex lens: positive power; concave lens: negative power.
For thin lenses in contact, P = P1 + P2; the combined focal length follows 1/f = 1/f1 + 1/f2.
concepts.real_life_example: Opticians write spectacle prescriptions in dioptres, such as +2.0 D for a converging reading lens and -1.5 D for a diverging distance lens.

worked_examples.title: Concave mirror: focal length and magnification
worked_examples.problem: An object is placed 10 cm in front of a concave mirror. A real image is formed 30 cm in front of the mirror. Find the focal length and the magnification.
solution: Step 1: Use the Cartesian sign convention. The object is in front of the mirror, so u = -10 cm.
Step 2: A real image in front of the mirror means v = -30 cm.
Step 3: Apply the mirror formula 1/f = 1/v + 1/u = -1/30 - 1/10.
Step 4: Take a common denominator of 30: -1/30 - 3/30 = -4/30, so f = -7.5 cm.
Step 5: Magnification m = -v/u = -(-30)/(-10) = -3.
Step 6: Negative f confirms a concave mirror; negative m means the image is real, inverted, and 3 times magnified.
worked_examples.answer: Focal length f = -7.5 cm (concave mirror); magnification m = -3, so the image is real, inverted, and 3 times larger.
worked_examples.board_tip: Write the sign convention explicitly before substituting; most lost marks come from using u = +10 cm.
worked_examples.exam_tip: Check the sign of f against the mirror type: concave negative, convex positive.

worked_examples.title: Convex mirror: image position and nature
worked_examples.problem: An object is placed 15 cm in front of a convex mirror of focal length 10 cm. Find the image distance and magnification.
solution: Step 1: Object distance u = -15 cm and, for a convex mirror, f = +10 cm.
Step 3: Take a common denominator of 30: 3/30 + 2/30 = 5/30 = 1/6.
Step 4: Therefore v = +6 cm. The positive sign means the image is behind the mirror.
Step 6: A positive magnification less than 1 means a virtual, erect, diminished image.
worked_examples.answer: Image distance v = +6 cm behind the mirror; m = +0.4, so the image is virtual, erect, and diminished.
worked_examples.board_tip: For a convex mirror, v is always positive, so the image is always behind the mirror and virtual.
worked_examples.exam_tip: A convex mirror never forms a real image of a real object.

worked_examples.title: Refractive index and speed of light in glass
worked_examples.problem: A ray of light travels from air into glass. The refractive index of glass with respect to air is 1.5 and the speed of light in air is 3 x 10^8 m/s. Find the speed of light in glass and the refractive index of air with respect to glass.
solution: Step 1: Absolute refractive index n = c/v, so v = c/n.
Step 3: The refractive index of air with respect to glass is n_air,glass = n_air / n_glass.
Step 4: Taking n_air = 1, n_air,glass = 1 / 1.5 = 0.67.
Step 5: Light slows down in glass, which is why it bends towards the normal.
worked_examples.answer: Speed of light in glass = 2 x 10^8 m/s; refractive index of air with respect to glass = 0.67.
worked_examples.board_tip: Keep the ratio the right way round: n_21 = n2 / n1, not n1 / n2.
worked_examples.exam_tip: The relative refractive index of a rarer medium with respect to a denser medium is less than 1.

worked_examples.title: Convex lens: image position and magnification
worked_examples.problem: An object is placed 30 cm in front of a convex lens of focal length 20 cm. Find the image distance, magnification, and nature of the image.
solution: Step 1: Use the Cartesian sign convention: u = -30 cm and f = +20 cm.
Step 3: Take a common denominator of 60: 3/60 - 2/60 = 1/60.
Step 4: Therefore v = +60 cm. The positive sign means the image is on the opposite side of the lens.
Step 6: A negative magnification with positive v means a real, inverted image twice the size of the object.
worked_examples.answer: Image distance v = +60 cm on the other side of the lens; m = -2, so the image is real, inverted, and 2 times magnified.
worked_examples.board_tip: For a lens, use 1/v - 1/u = 1/f. Do not mix it with the mirror formula, which has a plus sign.
worked_examples.exam_tip: A convex lens gives a real image when the object is beyond f and a virtual image when it is within f.

worked_examples.title: Power of two thin lenses in contact
worked_examples.problem: A convex lens of power +5 D is placed in contact with a concave lens of power -3 D. Find the power and focal length of the combination and state whether it converges or diverges.
solution: Step 1: For thin lenses in contact, the powers add: P = P1 + P2.
Step 3: Use P = 1/f with f in metres, so f = 1/P = 1/2 = 0.5 m.
Step 4: Convert to centimetres: f = 50 cm.
Step 5: A positive power means the combination behaves as a converging lens.
worked_examples.answer: P = +2 D; f = +0.5 m = +50 cm; the combination is converging.
worked_examples.board_tip: Powers add only when the lenses are in contact. If there is a gap, the simple addition rule does not apply.
worked_examples.exam_tip: Always convert focal length to metres before using P = 1/f.

problems.question: State the two laws of reflection of light.
solution: Step 1: The incident ray, the reflected ray, and the normal at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane.
Step 2: The angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection.
problems.final_answer: Both rays and the normal lie in one plane, and angle i = angle r.

problems.question: Define the principal focus of a concave mirror.
solution: Step 1: Consider rays parallel to the principal axis of a concave mirror.
Step 2: After reflection, these rays converge at a point on the principal axis.
Step 3: That point is called the principal focus of the concave mirror.
problems.final_answer: The principal focus is the point on the principal axis where rays parallel to the axis converge after reflection.

problems.question: An object is placed 20 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm. Find the image distance and magnification.
solution: Step 1: u = -20 cm and f = -10 cm.
problems.final_answer: v = -20 cm; m = -1, so the image is real, inverted, and the same size as the object.

problems.question: The refractive index of glass is 1.5. If the speed of light in air is 3 x 10^8 m/s, find the speed of light in glass.
solution: Step 1: Use n = c/v, so v = c/n.
Step 3: v = 2 x 10^8 m/s.
problems.final_answer: Speed of light in glass = 2 x 10^8 m/s.

problems.question: An object is placed 15 cm in front of a convex lens of focal length 10 cm. Find the image distance and magnification.
solution: Step 1: u = -15 cm and f = +10 cm.
problems.final_answer: v = +30 cm; m = -2, so the image is real, inverted, and 2 times magnified.

problems.question: Find the power of (i) a convex lens of focal length 50 cm and (ii) a concave lens of focal length 20 cm.
solution: Step 1: Convert focal lengths to metres: f1 = 0.50 m and f2 = -0.20 m.
Step 2: For the convex lens, P1 = 1/f1 = 1/0.50 = +2 D.
Step 3: For the concave lens, P2 = 1/f2 = 1/(-0.20) = -5 D.

solution: Step 1: A real image is inverted, so m = -3.

Step 3: m = v/u gives -3 = 45/u, so u = -15 cm.
problems.final_answer: Object distance u = -15 cm; focal length f = +11.25 cm (convex lens).

simple.question: According to the laws of reflection, the angle of incidence is always equal to the:

explanation.correct: The second law of reflection states that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.

wrong_options.0: Refraction involves a change of medium; the reflection law compares incidence and reflection.
wrong_options.2: The critical angle is a refraction concept, not the reflection law.
wrong_options.3: The angle of deviation is the net bend of a ray, not the reflected angle.

simple.question: The image formed by a plane mirror is:
options: Virtual, erect, and of the same size

explanation.correct: A plane mirror forms a virtual, erect image of the same size as the object.

wrong_options.0: A plane mirror does not form a real or enlarged image.
wrong_options.2: The image is erect, not inverted, and is not diminished.
wrong_options.3: The image is virtual, not real.

simple.question: A concave mirror can form:
options: Only images of the same size

explanation.correct: Depending on the object distance, a concave mirror can form real or virtual images.

wrong_options.0: When the object is within the focal length, the image is virtual.
wrong_options.1: When the object is beyond the focal length, the image is real.
wrong_options.3: Image size varies with object position.

simple.question: A convex mirror is used as a rear-view mirror because it:
options: Always forms an erect, diminished image and gives a wide field of view
Forms an inverted image of the same size
Has a very long focal length

explanation.correct: A convex mirror always forms a virtual, erect, diminished image and covers a wide field of view.

wrong_options.0: A convex mirror does not form a real image of a real object.
wrong_options.2: Its image is erect, not inverted.
wrong_options.3: Focal length is not the reason for its use.

simple.question: The focal length of a plane mirror is:

explanation.correct: A plane mirror has an infinite radius of curvature, so its focal length is taken as infinity.

wrong_options.0: Zero focal length would mean infinite power, which is not true here.
wrong_options.2: Focal length is a property of the mirror, not the object position.
wrong_options.3: Image distance changes with object distance; focal length does not.

simple.question: Refraction of light occurs because light:
options: Changes speed when it enters another medium

explanation.correct: A change in speed at the boundary of two media causes the ray to bend.

wrong_options.1: Absorption can reduce intensity but is not the cause of bending.
wrong_options.2: Reflection sends light back; refraction is transmission with bending.
wrong_options.3: Light carries energy; this does not explain refraction.

simple.question: The SI unit of the power of a lens is:

explanation.correct: Power is measured in dioptres, where 1 D = 1 m^-1.

wrong_options.0: Metre is the unit of length, not power.
wrong_options.2: Newton is the unit of force.
wrong_options.3: Watt is the unit of power in mechanics and electricity, not lens power.

simple.question: Which lens is a converging lens?

explanation.correct: A convex lens is thicker in the middle and converges parallel rays.

wrong_options.0: A concave lens is thinner in the middle and diverges rays.
wrong_options.2: A plane lens does not converge parallel rays.
wrong_options.3: A cylindrical lens produces line images and is not the standard converging lens.

simple.question: For a real, inverted image, the magnification is:

explanation.correct: The magnification of a real inverted image is negative by the sign convention.

wrong_options.0: Positive magnification corresponds to a virtual erect image.
wrong_options.2: Zero magnification would mean no image.
wrong_options.3: Magnification is 1 only for an image of the same size.

simple.question: The refractive index of vacuum is:

explanation.correct: By definition, the refractive index of vacuum is 1.

wrong_options.0: A refractive index of zero is not physically meaningful here.
wrong_options.2: 1.33 is approximately the refractive index of water.
wrong_options.3: An infinite refractive index would imply zero speed of light.

wrong_options.3: The image at infinity occurs for an object at the focus.

complex.question: A concave lens always forms an image that is:

explanation.correct: A concave lens diverges rays and always forms a virtual, erect, diminished image of a real object.

wrong_options.1: A concave lens does not form a real image of a real object.
wrong_options.2: The image is virtual, not real.
wrong_options.3: The image is erect, not inverted.

complex.question: An object is placed 30 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm. The image distance and magnification are:

wrong_options.1: A real image from a concave mirror has negative magnification.
wrong_options.2: The image is in front of the mirror, so v is negative.
wrong_options.3: These values would require a different object or focal length.

complex.question: Which pair of optical devices can form a real image of a real object?
options: Convex mirror and convex lens only

explanation.correct: A concave mirror and a convex lens can both converge rays to form a real image.

wrong_options.1: A convex mirror and a concave lens both diverge rays and form virtual images of real objects.
wrong_options.2: A plane mirror forms a virtual image, and a concave lens diverges.
wrong_options.3: A convex mirror alone cannot form a real image of a real object.

common_misconceptions.misconception: A concave mirror always forms a real image.
common_misconceptions.correction: A concave mirror forms a virtual, erect, magnified image when the object is between the pole and the focus.

common_misconceptions.misconception: A convex mirror can form a real image of a real object.
common_misconceptions.correction: A convex mirror always forms a virtual, erect, diminished image of a real object, whatever the object distance.
Magnification is negative for a real inverted image and positive for a virtual erect image.

common_misconceptions.misconception: The focal length of a spherical mirror is equal to its radius of curvature.
common_misconceptions.correction: The focal length is half the radius of curvature for a mirror of small aperture: f = R/2.

common_misconceptions.misconception: Light bends at a boundary because it reflects.
common_misconceptions.correction: Refraction occurs because the speed of light changes between media; reflection is a separate phenomenon at the boundary.

common_misconceptions.misconception: A higher refractive index means light travels faster in the medium.
common_misconceptions.correction: A higher refractive index means light travels more slowly, since n = c/v.

common_misconceptions.misconception: The lens formula is the same as the mirror formula.
common_misconceptions.correction: The lens formula is 1/v - 1/u = 1/f, while the mirror formula is 1/v + 1/u = 1/f.

common_misconceptions.misconception: Power of a lens is measured in watts.
common_misconceptions.correction: Power of a lens is measured in dioptres (D), where P = 1/f with f in metres.
